claim: Context-dependent memories may guide adaptive behavior relaying in previous experience while updating stored information through reconsolidation.
source: Context-dependent memories may guide adaptive behavior relaying in previous experience while updating stored information through reconsolidation.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's conceptual basis, drawing on established understanding of memory processes.

claim: mPFC 5-HT2aR controls retrieval and reconsolidation of object memories in the perirhinal cortex (PRH) in rats.
source: We found that mPFC 5-HT2aR controls retrieval and reconsolidation of object memories in the perirhinal cortex (PRH), but not in the dorsal hippocampus in rats.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: mPFC 5-HT2aR does not control retrieval and reconsolidation of object memories in the dorsal hippocampus in rats.
source: We found that mPFC 5-HT2aR controls retrieval and reconsolidation of object memories in the perirhinal cortex (PRH), but not in the dorsal hippocampus in rats.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Reconsolidation of objects memories in PRH required a functional interaction between the ventral hippocampus and the mPFC.
source: Also, reconsolidation of objects memories in PRH required a functional interaction between the ventral hippocampus and the mPFC.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: In the presence of conflicting information at retrieval, mPFC 5-HT2aR may facilitate top-down context-guided control over PRH to control the behavioral response and object memory reconsolidation.
source: Our results indicate that in the presence of conflicting information at retrieval, mPFC 5-HT2aR may facilitate top-down context-guided control over PRH to control the behavioral response and object memory reconsolidation.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings, involving inference from the data.

claim: Fear and associative conditioning has been used as a way to study the underlying circuits and molecular mechanisms of flexible memories through analysis of extinction, reversal learning and updating of contingencies in rodents.
source: In rodents, fear and associative conditioning has been used as a way to study the underlying circuits and molecular mechanisms of flexible memories through analysis of extinction, reversal learning and updating of contingencies (Lee et al., 2017; Rodriguez-Ortiz and Bermúdez-Rattoni, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the flexibility of episodic types of memory in spite of the evidence that the very process of remembering can affect memory stability.
source: However, little is known about the flexibility of episodic types of memory in spite of the evidence that the very process of remembering can affect memory stability.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, drawing on general scientific understanding.

claim: Reconsolidation is the process by which consolidated memories enter a new period of instability after reactivation.
source: Reconsolidation is the process by which consolidated memories enter a new period of instability after reactivation (Miranda and Bekinschtein, 2018; Nader et al., 2000) that can serve stabilization, strengthening, and updating (Lee et al., 2017; McKenzie and Eichenbaum, 2011; Rodriguez-Ortiz and Bermúdez-Rattoni, 2017).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reconsolidation can serve stabilization, strengthening, and updating of memories.
source: Reconsolidation is the process by which consolidated memories enter a new period of instability after reactivation (Miranda and Bekinschtein, 2018; Nader et al., 2000) that can serve stabilization, strengthening, and updating (Lee et al., 2017; McKenzie and Eichenbaum, 2011; Rodriguez-Ortiz and Bermúdez-Rattoni, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of reconsolidation have been extensively studied in animals using fear and appetitive conditioning and spatial learning tasks.
source: Its molecular mechanisms have been extensively studied in animals using fear and appetitive conditioning and spatial learning tasks (Nader, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Very little is known about the molecular and neural mechanisms of episodic memory reconsolidation.
source: However, very little is known about the molecular and neural mechanisms of episodic memory reconsolidation, consistently observed in human autobiographical memory (Forcato et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2003; Wymbs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Episodic memory reconsolidation is consistently observed in human autobiographical memory.
source: However, very little is known about the molecular and neural mechanisms of episodic memory reconsolidation, consistently observed in human autobiographical memory (Forcato et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2003; Wymbs et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interactions between PFC and hippocampus and other MTL structures may support the ability to create contextual representations, and use these contextual representations to retrieve the appropriate memories within a given context.
source: Interactions between PFC and hippocampus and other MTL structures may support the ability to create contextual representations, and use these contextual representations to retrieve the appropriate memories within a given context (Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Neurons from the MTL respond to specific objects and contexts.
source: Also neurons from the MTL respond to specific objects and contexts, suggesting that different areas may interact and work together to supportepisodic memory (Ahn and Lee, 2017; Brandman and Peelen, 2017; Davachi, 2006; Diana et al., 2007); Lee and Park, 2013c; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Squire et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different areas of the MTL may interact and work together to support episodic memory.
source: Also neurons from the MTL respond to specific objects and contexts, suggesting that different areas may interact and work together to supportepisodic memory (Ahn and Lee, 2017; Brandman and Peelen, 2017; Davachi, 2006; Diana et al., 2007); Lee and Park, 2013c; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Squire et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited literature about MTL function.

claim: Different MTL regions store parts of the representation of a particular episode.
source: Evidence indicates that different MTL regions store parts of the representation of a particular episode, and this raises the question of how this information is integrated, consolidated, retrieved, reactivated and reconsolidated.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about MTL function.

claim: The 5HT2a receptor (5-HT2aR) is one of the main post-synaptic serotoninergic receptor types and it is highly expressed in the PFC.
source: The 5HT2a receptor (5-HT2aR) is one of the main post-synaptic serotoninergic receptor types and it is highly expressed in the PFC.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neurobiological knowledge.

claim: A handful of studies suggest a role for 5-HT2aR in episodic memories in humans.
source: A handful of studies suggest a role for 5-HT2aR in episodic memories in humans (de Quervain et al., 2003; Wagner et al., 2008), and a few animal studies have addressed a potential role of 5-HT2aR during memory consolidation (Meneses, 2007; Meneses and Hong, 1997; Wagner et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A few animal studies have addressed a potential role of 5-HT2aR during memory consolidation.
source: A handful of studies suggest a role for 5-HT2aR in episodic memories in humans (de Quervain et al., 2003; Wagner et al., 2008), and a few animal studies have addressed a potential role of 5-HT2aR during memory consolidation (Meneses, 2007; Meneses and Hong, 1997; Wagner et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: mPFC 5-HT2aR plays a role in recognition memory retrieval.
source: We have previously shown that mPFC 5-HT2aR plays a role in recognition memory retrieval (Bekinschtein et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: 5-HT2aR activation is required when previously familiar and competing information is simultaneously presented.
source: Specifically, we demonstrated that 5-HT2aR activation is required when previously familiar and competing information is simultaneously presented.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from the authors' previous work.

claim: Infusion of MDL 11,939 (MDL) in the mPFC impaired the resolution of OIC during test 1, 24 hr after acquisition.
source: Similar to what we described for short-term memories (Bekinschtein et al., 2013), infusion of the 5-HT2aR specific antagonist MDL 11,939 (MDL) in the mPFC impaired the resolution of OIC during test 1, 24 hr after acquisition (Figure 1a, left panel).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: MDL effect on OIC resolution was transient as it did not affect the expression of the original object memories during test 2 in the MDL/VEH group.
source: MDL effect was transient as it did not affect the expression of the original object memories during test 2 in the MDL/VEH group (Figure 1a, right panel).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Infusion of EME immediately after test 1 disrupted long-term memory retention during test 2 in the VEH/EME group for the congruent object (object A) only.
source: Infusion of EME immediately after test 1 disrupted long-term memory retention during test 2 in the VEH/EME group for the congruent object (object A) only (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The memory trace for the congruent object was labilized in PRH during test 1.
source: This suggests that the memory trace for the congruent object was labilized in PRH during test 1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing EME effects.

claim: Blockade of mPFC 5-HT2aR during test 1 in combination with EME infusion into PRH immediately after test 1, disrupted long-term memory for both the incongruent (object B) and congruent (object A) objects during test 2.
source: However, blockade of mPFC 5-HT2aR during test 1 in combination with EME infusion into PRH immediately after test 1, disrupted long-term memory for both the incongruent (object B) and congruent (object A) objects, as observed in test 2 (Figure 1a, right panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Both memory traces (congruent and incongruent) were labilized becoming susceptible to the effects of EME when mPFC 5-HT2aR was blocked.
source: This suggests that both memory traces were labilized becoming susceptible to the effects of EME (Figure 1a, right panel).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing EME effects after MDL treatment.

claim: Total training exploration time did not differ between objects A and B.
source: Total training exploration time did not differ between objects A and B (paired t test, t = 0.078, p=0.9381, meanA = 48.99 ± 1.969, meanB = 49.16 ± 2.048).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of behavioral data from the training phase.

claim: There was a difference in exploration time between the first and second exposures to each context during training.
source: However, there was a difference in exploration time between the first and second exposures to each context during training (One-way ANOVA, F = 29,53, DF = 3, MS = 3968, pmain effect <0.0001; significant Bonferroni multiples comparisons, context1 (Tr1 vs Tr2) meanTr1 = 30.08 ± 1.461, meanTr2 = 19.93 ± 1.173, p<0.0001, context2 (Tr1 vs Tr2) meanTr1 = 30.27 ± 1.728, meanTr2 = 17.44 ± . 9589, p<0.0001), that was expected, after re-exposure to the same context object association.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of behavioral data from the training phase.

claim: Animals infused with EME have enhanced exploration of object A relative to the VEH group.
source: We found that animals infused with EME have enhanced exploration of object A relative to the VEH group, whereas there were no differences in the level of exploration of object B across groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2., panel a).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Animals infused with EME lost the memory for object A, they are not perceiving the novel object as familiar.
source: Thus, animals infused with EME lost the memory for object A, they are not perceiving the novel object as familiar.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data showing enhanced exploration of object A after EME treatment.

claim: Htr2a-/- mice had a deficit in the resolution of OIC task compared with Htr2a+/+ mice in test 1.
source: As previously reported (Morici et al., 2015a), Htr2a-/- mice had a deficit in the resolution of OIC task compared with Htr2a+/+ mice in test 1 (Figure 1b, left panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1b and cited previous work.

claim: Infusion of EME in the PRH immediately after test 1 impaired memory retention of the congruent object in Htr2a+/+ mice during test 2.
source: Infusion of EME in the PRH immediately after test 1 impaired memory retention of the congruent object in Htr2a+/+ mice and the retention of both the congruent and incongruent memory traces in Htr2a-/- during test 2 (Figure 1b, right panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Infusion of EME in the PRH immediately after test 1 impaired memory retention of both the congruent and incongruent memory traces in Htr2a-/- mice during test 2.
source: Infusion of EME in the PRH immediately after test 1 impaired memory retention of the congruent object in Htr2a+/+ mice and the retention of both the congruent and incongruent memory traces in Htr2a-/- during test 2 (Figure 1b, right panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Both the memories for the congruent and incongruent objects undergo reconsolidation in the PRH of Htr2a-/-, but only the congruent object memory reconsolidates in the PRH of Htr2a+/+ mice.
source: This result suggests that both the memories for the congruent and incongruent objects undergo reconsolidation in the PRH of Htr2a-/-, but only the congruent object memory reconsolidates in the PRH of Htr2a+/+ mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of EME in knockout versus wild-type mice.

claim: The absence of 5-HT2aR did not affect the integrity of the original memory, as Htr2a -/- mice infused with VEH were able to recognize effectively each object during test 2.
source: Interestingly, the absence of 5-HT2aR did not affect the integrity of the original memory, as Htr2a -/- mice infused with VEH were able to recognize effectively each object during test 2, suggesting that mPFC 5-HT2aR activation is involved in the selection of the memory traces to be reactivated and not in the storage of the memories per se.
evidence: This is an experimental finding and interpretation based on the performance of knockout mice with vehicle treatment.

claim: mPFC 5-HT2aR activation is involved in the selection of the memory traces to be reactivated and not in the storage of the memories per se.
source: Interestingly, the absence of 5-HT2aR did not affect the integrity of the original memory, as Htr2a -/- mice infused with VEH were able to recognize effectively each object during test 2, suggesting that mPFC 5-HT2aR activation is involved in the selection of the memory traces to be reactivated and not in the storage of the memories per se.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that knockout mice can still recognize objects despite retrieval deficits.

claim: Zif268/Egr1 is a transcription factor important for reconsolidation of different types of memories including recognition memory.
source: Zif268/Egr1 is a transcription factor important for reconsolidation of different types of memories including recognition memory (Veyrac et al., 2014), making it a good candidate to mediate reconsolidation in an OIC task.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: During test 2, the VEH/ASO group showed amnesia only for the congruent object, while the MDL/ASO group showed amnesia for both the congruent and incongruent objects.
source: During test 2, the VEH/ASO group showed amnesia only for the congruent object, while the MDL/ASO group showed amnesia for both the congruent and incongruent objects (Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Expression of Zif268 is necessary for object memory reconsolidation in PRH.
source: This result indicates that expression of Zif268 is necessary for object memory reconsolidation in PRH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of Zif268-ASO on memory retention.

claim: Infusion of Zif268-ASO significantly decreased Zif268 protein levels in PRH.
source: Infusion of Zif268-ASO significantly decreased Zif268 protein levels in PRH (Figure 1d, right panel).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Both groups exhibited comparable memory retention for the congruent object during test 2 when test 1 consisted of exposure to two copies of a congruent object.
source: Both groups exhibited comparable memory retention for the congruent object during test 2 (Figure 2a and Supplementary file 1), indicating that a contextual mismatch between what has been experienced during training and what is present during test 1 is required for labilization/reconsolidation of object memories (Hupbach et al., 2008; Pedreira et al., 2004; Sevenster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A contextual mismatch between what has been experienced during training and what is present during test 1 is required for labilization/reconsolidation of object memories.
source: Both groups exhibited comparable memory retention for the congruent object during test 2 (Figure 2a and Supplementary file 1), indicating that a contextual mismatch between what has been experienced during training and what is present during test 1 is required for labilization/reconsolidation of object memories (Hupbach et al., 2008; Pedreira et al., 2004; Sevenster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only the animals from the reactivated group infused with EME showed significantly lower memory retention for the congruent object during test 2.
source: Only the animals from the reactivated group infused with EME showed significantly lower memory retention for the congruent object during test 2 (Figure 2b left panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Novelty during memory retrieval during test 1 is a necessary step for reconsolidation of the OIC memory.
source: This result indicates that novelty during memory retrieval during test 1 is a necessary step for reconsolidation of the OIC memory and that object memories that are not retrieved are not susceptible to the action of protein synthesis inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of reactivated versus non-reactivated groups.

claim: Object memories that are not retrieved are not susceptible to the action of protein synthesis inhibitors.
source: This result indicates that novelty during memory retrieval during test 1 is a necessary step for reconsolidation of the OIC memory and that object memories that are not retrieved are not susceptible to the action of protein synthesis inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of reactivated versus non-reactivated groups.

claim: Infusion of EME into PRH immediately after exposure to the context alone (test 1) was enough to cause amnesia for the contextually congruent object but not for the incongruent object in test 2.
source: We found that infusion of EME into PRH immediately after exposure to the context alone (test 1) was enough to cause amnesia for the contextually congruent object (Figure 3a, right panel and Supplementary file 1), but not for the incongruent object in test 2.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The context cue can drive the labilization of the memory for objects previously associated with it.
source: This result suggests that the context cue can drive the labilization of the memory for objects previously associated with it, and that retrieval and reactivation of object memories in PRH is context-guided.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that context alone can trigger reconsolidation.

claim: Retrieval and reactivation of object memories in PRH is context-guided.
source: This result suggests that the context cue can drive the labilization of the memory for objects previously associated with it, and that retrieval and reactivation of object memories in PRH is context-guided.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that context alone can trigger reconsolidation.

claim: Infusion of EME into the PRH after test 1 did not produce any deficit in memory retention for any of the objects during test 2 when objects were presented in a context not associated with them.
source: As predicted, infusion of EME into the PRH after test 1 did not produce any deficit in memory retention for any of the objects during test 2 (Figure 3b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Presentation of both objects in a context not associated with them was not enough for reconsolidation of object memories in PRH.
source: Thus, presentation of both objects in a context not associated with them was not enough for reconsolidation of object memories in PRH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of EME effect when objects are presented in a non-associated context.

claim: Both groups, independently of the manipulation of the mPFC spent more time exploring the novel object compared with the congruent object during test 1 when the incongruent object was swapped for a novel object.
source: We found that both groups, independently of the manipulation of the mPFC spent more time exploring the novel object compared with the congruent object during test 1 (Figure 3c, left panel).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Infusion of EME immediately after test 1 blocked the reconsolidation of the congruent trace independently of the infusion of MDL or vehicle in the mPFC when the incongruent object was replaced by a novel object.
source: Infusion of EME immediately after test 1 blocked the reconsolidation of the congruent trace independently of the infusion of MDL or vehicle in the mPFC (Figure 3c, right panel and Supplementary file 1), but had no effect on the reconsolidation of the incongruent object.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In the absence of the incongruent object, serotoninergic modulation of mPFC 5-HT2aR was not necessary to solve the task.
source: This result suggests that in the absence of the incongruent object, serotoninergic modulation of mPFC 5-HT2aR was not necessary to solve the task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that MDL had no effect when a novel object replaced the incongruent object.

claim: mPFC 5-HT2aR signaling might have a selective role in conditions in which correct retrieval is the consequence of recognizing a particular combination of an object and a context.
source: mPFC 5-HT2aR signaling might have a selective role in conditions in which correct retrieval is the consequence of recognizing a particular combination of an object and a context.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the pattern of results across different experimental conditions.

claim: Pharmacological studies indicate that the functionality of the dorsal hippocampus (dHPC) is required for the correct resolution of the OIC task.
source: Pharmacological studies indicate that the functionality of the dorsal hippocampus (dHPC) is required for the correct resolution of the OIC task (Bekinschtein et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Protein synthesis in the CA1 region of the hippocampus has been shown to be necessary for object recognition memory reconsolidation.
source: Also, protein synthesis in the CA1 region of the hippocampus has been shown to be necessary for object recognition memory reconsolidation (Balderas et al., 2015; Clarke et al., 2010; Radiske et al., 2017; Rossato et al., 2015; Sachser et al., 2016; Winters et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MDL infusion into mPFC before test 1 impaired performance in the OIC task.
source: As expected, MDL infusion into mPFC before test 1 impaired performance in the OIC task (Figure 4a, left panel).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Blockade of dCA1 protein synthesis after test 1 affected memory retention for the incongruent object without impairing the retention of the congruent object.
source: However, blockade of dCA1 protein synthesis after test 1 affected memory retention for the incongruent object without impairing the retention of the congruent object.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the dCA1 EME infusion experiment.

claim: The effect of dCA1 protein synthesis blockade on memory retention was independent of the blockade of mPFC 5-HT2aR.
source: This effect was independent of the blockade of mPFC 5-HT2aR.
evidence: This is an experimental finding showing no interaction between MDL and EME effects in dCA1.

claim: The incongruent, but not the congruent, trace is reactivated in the dCA1 during test 1 in a mPFC 5-HT2aR-independent way.
source: Unexpectedly, our result suggests that the incongruent, but not the congruent, trace is reactivated in the dCA1 during test 1 in a mPFC 5-HT2aR-independent way (Figure 4a, right panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the selective effect of EME on the incongruent object in dCA1.

claim: Novelty is needed for reconsolidation in the dHPC.
source: We observed that the infusion of EME had no effect on reconsolidation of the congruent or the incongruent objects, suggesting that novelty is also needed for reconsolidation in the dHPC (Figure 4b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of EME effect when no novelty is present during test 1.

claim: Animals infused with Zif268-ASO into the dCA1 before test 1 showed a significantly lower recognition of the incongruent object during test 2, but not of the congruent object compared with MSO-infused animals.
source: Animals infused with ASO into the dCA1 before test 1 showed a significantly lower recognition of the incongruent object during test 2, but not of the congruent object compared with MSO-infused animals (Figure 4c, right panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Amnesia for the incongruent object after Zif268-ASO infusion in dCA1 was specific and independent of the blockade of 5HT2aR in the mPFC.
source: Consistent with our findings using EME, amnesia was specific for the incongruent object and independent of the blockade of 5HT2aR in the mPFC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of Zif268-ASO effects in dCA1.

claim: Zif268 participates in reconsolidation of the incongruent memory trace in dCA1.
source: This result indicates that Zif268 participates in reconsolidation of the incongruent memory trace in dCA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of Zif268-ASO on memory retention in dCA1.

claim: Zif268-ASO decreased Zif268 levels in dCA1.
source: As expected, Zif268-ASO decreased Zif268 levels (Figure 4d, right panel).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The ventral but not the dorsal hippocampus has direct unidirectional connections with mPFC.
source: However, the ventral but not the dorsal hippocampus has direct unidirectional connections with mPFC (Swanson et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous anatomical literature.

claim: Silencing the vCA1 region during test 1 resulted in reconsolidation of the congruent and incongruent memory traces.
source: Silencing the vCA1 region during test 1 resulted in reconsolidation of the congruent and incongruent memory traces, while when the vCA1 region was active, only the congruent memory trace was sensitive to EME infusion. (Figure 5a Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: When the vCA1 region was active, only the congruent memory trace was sensitive to EME infusion.
source: Silencing the vCA1 region during test 1 resulted in reconsolidation of the congruent and incongruent memory traces, while when the vCA1 region was active, only the congruent memory trace was sensitive to EME infusion. (Figure 5a Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Blockade of vCA1 activity had no effect on memory retention in test 2 when animals were trained in SNOR.
source: Importantly, if animals were trained in SNOR, which does not require integration of object and context, blockade of vCA1 activity had no effect on memory retention in test 2 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: vCA1 activity is necessary during retrieval for discrimination between the congruent and incongruent objects, but not for object recognition per se.
source: This set of results indicates that vCA1 activity is necessary during retrieval for discrimination between the congruent and incongruent objects, but not for object recognition per se.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of vCA1 inactivation in OIC versus SNOR tasks.

claim: Ipsilateral blockade of 5-HT2aR signaling and vCA1 activity had no effect on retrieval of OIC task during test 1.
source: We found that ipsilateral blockade of 5-HT2aR signaling and vCA1 activity had no effect on retrieval of OIC task during test 1.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the disconnection experiment.

claim: When the same manipulation was done contralaterally, the congruent and incongruent objects were explored equally, indicating a memory deficit.
source: However, when the same manipulation was done contralaterally, the congruent and incongruent objects were explored equally, indicating a memory deficit (Figure 5c, left panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The ipsilateral manipulation resulted in sensitivity to EME for the congruent object memory trace only, while the contralateral manipulation resulted in EME-dependent amnesia for both the congruent and incongruent objects.
source: During test 2, the ipsilateral manipulation resulted in sensitivity to EME for the congruent object memory trace only, while the contralateral manipulation resulted in EME-dependent amnesia for both the congruent and incongruent objects (Figure 5c, right panel and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Activity in the vCA1 interacts with 5-HT2aR-dependent activity in the mPFC to control context-guided retrieval and reconsolidation of object memories in PRH.
source: Thus, these observations suggest that activity in the vCA1 interacts with 5-HT2aR-dependent activity in the mPFC to control context-guided retrieval and reconsolidation of object memories in PRH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the disconnection experiment results.

claim: OIC memories reconsolidate at least in two structures, PRH and dCA1.
source: Our main findings are that (1) OIC memories reconsolidate at least in two structures, PRH and dCA1; (2) context guides reconsolidation of object memories in PRH and this process is sensitive to mPFC 5-HT2aR modulation; (3) context-guided reconsolidation of object memories in dCA1 is independent of mPFC 5-HT2aR activation; (4) Zif268 is required for context-guided reconsolidation of object memories in both structures; and (5) functional interaction between vCA1 and mPFC is necessary during retrieval to control context-guided reconsolidation in PRH.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Context guides reconsolidation of object memories in PRH and this process is sensitive to mPFC 5-HT2aR modulation.
